propositions.text: The Appellant alleges a fear of persecution in India due to his Muslim religion.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX ("the Appellant") alleges a fear of persecution in India due to his Muslim religion.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims he fears persecution in India because he is Muslim.

propositions.text: Muslim fanatics threatened the Appellant due to his friendship with Hindus, believing he converted to Hinduism.
propositions.quote: Muslim fanatics made threatening phone calls to him because of his friendship with Hindus. Fearing for his safety, he discontinued his friendship with Hindus, however, Muslim fanatics believed that he had converted to Hinduism and continued to threaten him.

propositions.text: Muslim fanatics told Hindus the Appellant made false statements about their gods, leading to harassment from both groups.
propositions.quote: The Muslim fanatics told local Hindus that the Appellant had made false statements about their gods and so he was harassed by Muslims and Hindus through threatening phone calls.

propositions.text: A mob of RSS Hindu fanatics threatened to kill the Appellant if he returned to India, and police dispersed the mob.
propositions.quote: a mob of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) Hindu fanatics surrounded the Appellant's house in India and told his family that they would kill the Appellant if they saw him. Police were called and they dispersed the mob.

propositions.text: The Appellant's family continued to receive threats, and his wife advised him not to return to India, leading to his refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's family continued to receive threatening calls from the RSS Hindu fanatics about the Appellant. The Muslim community started making insulting religious comments about the Appellant to his family. The Appellant's wife told the Appellant not to return to India as a result of these problems. The Appellant then filed a claim for refugee protection in June of 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges threats and harassment from both Muslims and Hindus, leading to his refugee claim after continued threats and police involvement.

propositions.text: The RPD denied the claim, finding a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denied the claim. It found that the Appellant has a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Jaipur or New Delhi.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD denied the claim, finding the Appellant has a viable IFA in Jaipur or New Delhi.

propositions.text: On appeal, the Appellant submits that the RPD made a number of errors.
propositions.quote: On appeal, the Appellants submit that the RPD made a number of errors.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD made several errors.

propositions.text: The RPD was correct in its assessment of the evidence and IFA analysis.
propositions.quote: Having found that the RPD was correct in its assessment of the evidence and its IFA analysis,

propositions.text: The decision of the RPD dismissing the appeal is confirmed.
propositions.quote: I am confirming the decision of the RPD dismissing the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the RPD's assessment correct and confirms the dismissal of the appeal.

propositions.text: RAD reviews RPD decisions on a standard of correctness for law, fact, and mixed fact and law, except for oral testimony assessment.
propositions.quote: the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is to review decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness on questions of law, fact, and mixed fact and law, after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases may attract a standard of review of reasonableness.

propositions.text: Unless otherwise stated, a correctness standard has been applied in this decision.
propositions.quote: Unless otherwise stated, a correctness standard has been applied.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies a correctness standard except for oral testimony, and this standard is used here unless otherwise stated.

propositions.text: The Appellant submitted three affidavits, a CD of 16 video clips, and 13 news articles as proposed new evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant tendered the following items as proposed new evidence in support of his appeal. a) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX;3 b) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX;4 c) Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX;5 d) Compact disc containing 16 video clips of news reports with an attached list giving a brief description of the videos;6 and e) 13 news articles.7

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant submitted affidavits, video clips, and news articles as new evidence for his appeal.

propositions.text: Affidavits (a)-(c) meet IRPA s.110(4) as they could not have been obtained before the hearing despite efforts.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that items (a) to (c) meet the statutory requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) because they could not have been made available during his hearing despite his efforts to obtain them.

propositions.text: Documents (d) and (e) are recent video clips and news articles about attacks on Muslims, many post-dating the hearing.
propositions.quote: He points out that the documents in items (d) and (e) are video clips and news articles of recent attacks on Muslims in Delhi, Jaipur, and other parts of India. He also points out that many of the incidents reported in the video clips and articles took place subsequent to his hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues affidavits could not be obtained earlier and that the video/news evidence concerns recent attacks on Muslims after his hearing.

propositions.text: Under IRPA s.110(4), only evidence arising after rejection or not reasonably available at the time may be presented on appeal.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of his claim or that was not reasonably available, or that he could not reasonably have been expected8 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

propositions.text: The Appellant must make detailed submissions on how new evidence meets s.110(4) and relates to him.
propositions.quote: It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in his Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to him.

paragraphs.summary: The law limits new evidence to what arose after rejection or was unavailable, and the Appellant must explain how it meets these requirements.

propositions.text: If new evidence meets s.110(4), the RAD applies the adapted Raza factors (credibility, relevance, newness) per Singh, not materiality.
propositions.quote: In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD is not to consider the fourth Raza factor of materiality to the admission of new evidence, which is a consideration for subsection 110(6) and the request for an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: If evidence meets s.110(4), the RAD assesses credibility, relevance, and newness, not materiality, per Singh and Raza.

propositions.text: Affidavits (a)-(c) are not relevant to the determinative issue of IFA and are rejected as new evidence.
propositions.quote: However, the documents fail the relevance factor of Singh and Raza, as they are not related to the determinative issue of IFA. ... Accordingly, items (a), (b) and (c) are rejected.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted the Appellant's allegations for IFA determination, including the XXXX XXXX, 2017 event, despite credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: for the purpose of its determination on IFA, it accepted his allegations, including the alleged XXXX XXXX, 2017 event.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal rejects the affidavits as irrelevant to IFA, noting the RPD accepted the Appellant's allegations for IFA purposes.

propositions.text: Video clips and news articles (d) and (e), except those predating rejection, meet s.110(4) and are accepted as new evidence.
propositions.quote: Items (d) and (e), excluding video clips and news articles published prior to the rejection,12 meet the statutory requirements of subsection 110(4). ... Items (d) and (e), excluding the portions predating the rejection mentioned above, are accepted as new evidence in this appeal.

propositions.text: A further assessment of this new evidence will be provided below.
propositions.quote: A further assessment of this evidence is found below.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal accepts the post-rejection video clips and news articles as new evidence and will assess them further.

propositions.text: The Appellant requests an oral hearing, claiming an interpretation error led to a credibility loss and was a major reason for rejection.
propositions.quote: He maintains that an interpretation error was made during the hearing, he lost credibility due to the error, and it was one of the major reasons his claim was rejected.

propositions.text: The Appellant claims he lost the chance to clarify that his wife received threats after the 2017 incident.
propositions.quote: He maintains that he lost the opportunity to make clear that his wife received threats subsequent to the XXXX XXXX, 2017 incident.

propositions.text: An oral hearing requires admissible new evidence raising a serious, central, and determinative credibility issue.
propositions.quote: My jurisdiction to convene an oral hearing is limited: there must be admissible new evidence that raises a serious issue of credibility, is central, and determinative.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant requests an oral hearing due to alleged interpretation error, but the tribunal notes strict criteria for granting such a hearing.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges an interpretation error led to a determinative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleges that an interpretation error led to a credibility finding which was determinative of his claim.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted the Appellant's allegations for IFA purposes, so credibility was not determinative as alleged.
propositions.quote: The credibility finding was not determinative as the Appellant alleges.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims an interpretation error affected credibility, but the tribunal finds credibility was not determinative for the IFA decision.

propositions.text: The new evidence does not justify allowing the claim or convening an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: The new evidence does not justify allowing the Appellant's refugee protection claim for the reasons that follow. The Appellant's request for an oral hearing is therefore denied.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the new evidence insufficient to allow the claim or grant an oral hearing.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted the Appellant's persecution allegations but found he failed to show persecutors could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: It found however that the Appellant had failed to establish that his persecutors would locate him in a different city.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's evidence about being found in a new city speculative and vague, and that police would struggle to locate someone outside their home state.
propositions.quote: It noted evidence indicating that it is difficult to locate individuals in India once they move outside of a particular state, and even police would in almost all cases be unable to locate someone outside of their home state.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant failed to establish that the mob or callers could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: As a result, the RPD found that the Appellant had failed to establish that the individuals who made threatening phone calls or the individuals who formed the mob could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD accepted the Appellant's allegations but found he failed to show persecutors could find him in Jaipur or New Delhi.

propositions.text: The Appellant maintains Hindu fundamentalists can trace him anywhere in India due to systemic flaws and inefficient policing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant maintains that he will be traced by Hindu fundamentalists wherever he goes in India due to loopholes in the system and inefficient policing.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues new evidence shows recent attacks on Muslims in Delhi, Jaipur, and other parts of India, with law enforcement siding with Hindu fundamentalists.
propositions.quote: He points out that his new evidence shows that there have been recent attacks on Muslims in Delhi, Jaipur, and other parts of India; law enforcement agencies side with the majority Hindu fundamentalists; and Hindu fundamentalists have tentacles all over India.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues he can be traced anywhere in India and cites new evidence of recent attacks and biased law enforcement.

propositions.text: The RPD was not wrong to find the Appellant failed to show persecutors could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: In my view, the RPD was not wrong to find that the Appellant had failed to establish that the individuals who made threatening phone calls or the individuals who formed the mob around his house could locate him in Jaipur or New Delhi.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to establish that these individuals would pursue him to one of the proposed IFAs.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant failed to establish that these individuals would pursue him to one of the proposed IFAs.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the Appellant failed to show persecutors could find or pursue him in Jaipur or New Delhi.

propositions.text: The Appellant's problems were localized to Hyderabad and no credible evidence shows these would follow him to Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: The problems the Appellant encountered in India were localized and no credible evidence was presented to indicate that these problems would follow the Appellant to Jaipur or New Delhi.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the Appellant's problems were localized and not shown to follow him to the proposed IFAs.

propositions.text: Communal violence between Hindus and Muslims is regular in India, but not so widespread as to make the proposed IFAs unreasonable.
propositions.quote: these tensions are not so widespread, omnipresent and severe as to render the proposed IFAs objectively unreasonable for the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds that, despite regular communal violence, the proposed IFAs are not unreasonable for the Appellant.

propositions.text: Communal violence cited by the Appellant does not rise to a serious possibility of persecution or risk under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: the communal violence referred to by the Appellant does not rise to a serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm under sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Many Muslims live and work in the proposed IFAs, and the Appellant has not shown his problems would follow him there.
propositions.quote: There are many Muslims living and working in each of the proposed IFAs, and the Appellant has not established that his problems would follow him to either location.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds that communal violence does not meet the threshold for persecution or risk, and the Appellant's problems would not follow him to the IFAs.

propositions.text: There is not a serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm for the Appellant in Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: I conclude that there is not a serious possibility of the Appellant being persecuted in Jaipur or New Delhi or that on a balance of probabilities, he would be subjected to a danger of torture or a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in either of these places.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal concludes there is no serious risk of persecution or harm for the Appellant in Jaipur or New Delhi.

propositions.text: Objective country conditions evidence shows it is reasonable for the Appellant to relocate within India.
propositions.quote: the objective country conditions evidence establishes on a balance of probabilities, that it is reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to a different city in India.

propositions.text: India is large, with over 1.2 billion people, seven cities over 5 million, and 172.2 million Muslims, some areas with Muslim majorities.
propositions.quote: India is a very large country with a population of over 1.2 billion. It noted that there are seven cities that have a population of over 5 million. It noted that there are approximately 172.2 million Muslims in India, and some parts of India have a Muslim majority.

propositions.text: No legal controls prevent movement throughout India.
propositions.quote: there are no legal controls preventing the movement of people throughout India.

propositions.text: The Appellant could live freely as a Muslim in another Indian city.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant would be able to live freely as a Muslim in another city in India.

propositions.text: Given the Appellant's circumstances and the high threshold for IFA unreasonableness, he has not shown relocation would be unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Given the Appellant's circumstances, including his age and professional background, the large Muslim population spread throughout the country, and the high threshold for the unreasonableness of an IFA, the RPD found that the Appellant had not discharged the burden for establishing that relocating would be unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found, based on country evidence and the Appellant's circumstances, that relocation within India is reasonable and not unduly harsh.

propositions.text: The Appellant has a degree from an Indian university, worked as an architect for ten years, and was a business partner.
propositions.quote: the Appellant has a XXXX XXXX XXXXdegree from a university in India. He worked as an architect for approximately ten years, and then was a partner in a business.

propositions.text: The Appellant is forty, has traveled to Saudi Arabia, and adapted to life in Canada for over five years.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is forty years old, has travelled to Saudi Arabia,17 and has shown that he was able to adapt and support himself in Canada for over five years.

propositions.text: The Appellant has more than basic skills to find employment or start a business and could adapt to a new environment in India.
propositions.quote: This points to the fact that the Appellant has more than the basic skills that could be used to find employment or establish a business and that he would be able to adapt to a new environment within India.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal notes the Appellant's education, work experience, adaptability, and skills support his ability to relocate and adapt within India.

propositions.text: The Appellant's only reason against relocation is communal tensions and violence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not expressed any reason why it would be unduly harsh for him to relocate to Jaipur or New Delhi, except for communal tensions and violence.

propositions.text: Country documentation shows communal tensions are regular but not so widespread or intense as to make relocation unreasonable for the Appellant.
propositions.quote: although they are regular occurrences, they are not so widespread or intense as to make it unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to one of those cities, where many other Muslims live and work.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the Appellant's only objection is communal violence, but country evidence shows this does not make relocation unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RPD was not wrong to find the Appellant had not shown relocation would be unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the RPD was not wrong to find that the Appellant had not discharged the burden for establishing that relocating would be unreasonable.

propositions.text: Upon reviewing the evidence, the tribunal finds the same as the RPD.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the evidence, I find the same.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to prove it would be unreasonable or unduly harsh to relocate to Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the Appellant has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that it would be unreasonable or unduly harsh for him to relocate to Jaipur or New Delhi.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal agrees with the RPD that the Appellant has not shown relocation would be unreasonable or unduly harsh.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err regarding the availability of an IFA; its decision is correct.
propositions.quote: the RPD did not err regarding the availability of an IFA. Its decision is correct.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm if relocated to Jaipur or New Delhi.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the Appellant failed to establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution, or that on a balance of probabilities, he would be subjected to a danger of torture or a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he relocates to Jaipur or New Delhi.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not establish that relocation to Jaipur or New Delhi would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh.
propositions.quote: the Appellant did not establish that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for him to relocate to either of these places.

propositions.text: This finding is determinative of the appeal.
propositions.quote: This finding is determinative of the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the RPD's IFA decision correct and concludes the Appellant failed to show risk or unreasonableness in relocating, determining the appeal.

propositions.text: The determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection is confirmed; the appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I confirm the determination of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal confirms the RPD's decision and dismisses the Appellant's appeal.
